title: Properties and Changes of Matter
unitGoal: Students will describe matter by its properties, compare physical and chemical changes, and investigate mixtures, solutions, and changes of state.

lessons.title: Describing Matter by Its Properties
lessons.learningGoal: Students will describe matter using observable and measurable properties instead of opinions or guesses.
successCriteria: I can explain what matter is.
I can describe a material using properties such as colour, texture, hardness, flexibility, magnetism, and solubility.
I can choose properties that help compare or identify materials.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise describing matter by observable and measurable properties.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that matter has properties and that careful property descriptions are stronger than opinions or guesses.
lessons.christianFocus: Matter is part of God's created world. Students should describe it honestly and carefully, using evidence rather than guesses.
lessonContent: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space.
A property is a feature that can be observed or measured.
Physical properties include state, colour, texture, hardness, flexibility, magnetism, transparency, mass, volume, and solubility.
A scientific description should tell what can be noticed or measured, not just whether someone likes the material.
More than one property is often needed to compare or identify a material.

studentActivity.title: Matter Properties Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise describing and comparing materials by their properties.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: matter has properties
steps.text: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. A property is a feature you can observe or measure. Useful property words help someone else understand the material clearly.

steps.title: Property, Not Opinion
steps.prompt: Use careful science words
steps.text: A property might be colour, texture, hardness, flexibility, magnetism, transparency, mass, volume, or solubility. An opinion, such as 'nice' or 'boring,' does not describe the material scientifically.

steps.title: Choose a Property
steps.prompt: Which sentence describes a property of a material?
choices: The strip bends without breaking.
The strip would make a good bookmark.
The strip reminds me of a toy.
steps.feedback: Correct. Flexibility is a property that can be observed.
steps.hint: Look for the choice that tells what the material does or is like.

steps.title: Magnet Test
steps.prompt: A shiny grey object is attracted to a magnet. Which property is being tested?
choices: magnetism
solubility
transparency
steps.feedback: Yes. Attraction to a magnet is a magnetic property.
steps.hint: A magnet helps test one specific property.

steps.title: Careful Description
steps.prompt: Which description is most useful in science?
choices: The material is transparent and smooth.
The material is probably expensive.
The material looks like something from a drawer.
steps.correctAnswer: The material is transparent and smooth.
steps.feedback: Correct. It uses properties that can be checked.
steps.hint: Useful descriptions can be observed by another person.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A property should be based on what can be observed or measured, not just personal liking.
choices: True
False
steps.feedback: Correct. Scientific descriptions need careful evidence.
steps.hint: Think about what another person could check.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised choosing useful property words.

steps.title: Properties Help Us Compare
steps.prompt: One property may not be enough
steps.text: Two materials can look alike but behave differently. If two powders are both white, solubility, texture, or reaction with a safe test may help tell them apart.

steps.title: Powder Comparison
steps.prompt: Two white powders look similar. One dissolves in water, and the other settles at the bottom. Which property helps tell them apart?
choices: solubility
colour
shape of the cup
steps.feedback: Correct. Solubility describes whether a substance dissolves.
steps.hint: The sentence is about dissolving in water.

steps.title: Measuring Mass
steps.prompt: Which tool would best help compare the mass of two samples?
choices: a balance
a thermometer
a hand lens
steps.feedback: Yes. A balance compares or measures mass.
steps.hint: Mass is not measured by how clear or warm something is.

steps.title: Transparency
steps.prompt: Which observation compares transparency?
choices: One sample lets light pass clearly, while the other blocks most light.
One sample is heavier than the other sample.
One sample dissolves faster in warm water.
steps.correctAnswer: One sample lets light pass clearly, while the other blocks most light.
steps.feedback: Correct. Transparency is about how light passes through.
steps.hint: Think about clear, cloudy, or opaque materials.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Two objects can share some properties and still differ in other properties.
choices: True
False
steps.feedback: Correct. Materials can be alike in one way and different in another.
steps.hint: For example, two objects may be blue but have different masses.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised using properties to compare materials.

quiz.title: Describing Matter by Its Properties Quiz

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes matter?
choices: Anything that has mass and takes up space.
Only things that are hard enough to hold.
Only materials that can be seen from across a room.
questions.correctAnswer: Anything that has mass and takes up space.

questions.prompt: Which is a physical property?
choices: whether a material is flexible
whether a student likes the material
whether the material is useful for a craft
questions.reviewNote: Flexibility is a property that can be tested.

questions.prompt: A paper clip is attracted to a magnet. Which property is shown?
choices: magnetism
transparency
solubility
questions.reviewNote: Magnetism is tested with a magnet.

questions.prompt: What does solubility describe?
choices: whether a substance dissolves in another substance
whether a substance can be bent into a new shape
whether a substance lets light pass through it
questions.correctAnswer: whether a substance dissolves in another substance

questions.prompt: Which description is most scientific?
choices: The fabric is rough and dark blue.
The fabric would look best on a poster.
The fabric seems like something from a store.
questions.correctAnswer: The fabric is rough and dark blue.

questions.prompt: Which tool is best for comparing mass?
choices: balance
ruler
magnet

questions.prompt: An opinion can replace a property when describing a material scientifically.
choices: True
False
questions.reviewNote: Scientific descriptions should use observable or measurable properties.

questions.prompt: A material may need more than one property to be identified carefully.
choices: True
False
questions.reviewNote: Several properties can give stronger evidence.

lessons.title: Solids, Liquids, and Gases
lessons.learningGoal: Students will compare solids, liquids, and gases by shape, volume, and particle behaviour.
successCriteria: I can describe solids, liquids, and gases.
I can explain how shape and volume help identify a state of matter.
I can use a simple particle model to compare states of matter.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise comparing solids, liquids, and gases using shape, volume, and a simple particle model.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that matter can be solid, liquid, or gas and that the state of matter affects how a material behaves.
lessons.christianFocus: Students can notice order and patterns in God's created world as they compare different states of matter.
lessonContent: A state of matter describes whether a material is a solid, liquid, or gas.
A solid usually keeps its own shape and volume.
A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container.
A gas spreads out to fill the space available and can often be compressed more easily than a liquid or solid.
A simple particle model helps explain why solids, liquids, and gases behave differently.

studentActivity.title: States of Matter Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise comparing solids, liquids, and gases.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: three common states
steps.text: Matter is often described as a solid, liquid, or gas. Shape and volume are two helpful clues for telling the states apart.

steps.title: Shape and Volume
steps.prompt: Use both clues
steps.text: A solid usually keeps its own shape and volume. A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container. A gas spreads out to fill the space available.

steps.title: Solid Clue
steps.prompt: Which statement best describes a solid block of wax?
choices: It keeps its own shape and volume.
It keeps its volume but takes the shape of any container.
It spreads out to fill all available space.
steps.correctAnswer: It keeps its own shape and volume.
steps.feedback: Correct. A solid usually keeps its shape and volume.
steps.hint: Think about whether it flows or spreads out.

steps.title: Liquid Clue
steps.prompt: Water is poured from a cup into a bowl. What usually changes?
choices: the shape of the water
the material the water is made of
the fact that it has volume
steps.feedback: Yes. A liquid takes the shape of its container.
steps.hint: The water is still water.

steps.title: Gas Clue
steps.prompt: Which statement best describes air inside a balloon?
choices: It spreads out inside the space of the balloon.
It keeps a cube shape after entering the balloon.
It has no connection to matter because it cannot be held by hand.
steps.correctAnswer: It spreads out inside the space of the balloon.
steps.feedback: Correct. A gas spreads out to fill the space available.
steps.hint: Air is matter even though it can be hard to see.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A liquid usually keeps its own shape after it is poured into a different container.
choices: True
False
steps.feedback: Correct. A liquid usually takes the shape of its container.
steps.hint: Liquids flow.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised using shape and volume clues.

steps.title: Particles Explain Behaviour
steps.prompt: A simple model helps
steps.text: In a simple particle model, particles in a solid are close together and mostly vibrate in place. Particles in a liquid are close but can slide past one another. Particles in a gas are farther apart and move freely.

steps.title: Solid Particles
steps.prompt: Which particle description best fits a solid?
choices: Particles are packed closely and mostly vibrate in place.
Particles are far apart and fill any space available.
Particles slide past each other and take the container's shape.
steps.correctAnswer: Particles are packed closely and mostly vibrate in place.
steps.feedback: Correct. Solid particles are close together.
steps.hint: A solid keeps its shape.

steps.title: Liquid Particles
steps.prompt: Why can a liquid be poured?
choices: Its particles can slide past one another.
Its particles stay locked in one fixed shape.
Its particles disappear when the container changes.
steps.correctAnswer: Its particles can slide past one another.
steps.feedback: Yes. Liquid particles can move past each other.
steps.hint: Pouring means the material can flow.

steps.title: Gas Particles
steps.prompt: Why can a gas spread through a container?
choices: Its particles are farther apart and move freely.
Its particles are joined in a fixed pattern.
Its particles become solid when they touch air.
steps.correctAnswer: Its particles are farther apart and move freely.
steps.feedback: Correct. Gas particles move freely and spread out.
steps.hint: Think about air filling a balloon.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A simple particle model can help explain why the same matter behaves differently in different states.
choices: True
False
steps.feedback: Correct. Particle spacing and movement help explain state behaviour.
steps.hint: Models help explain patterns we observe.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised comparing particles in solids, liquids, and gases.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a solid?
choices: It usually keeps its own shape and volume.
It keeps its volume but always changes its shape.
It spreads out to fill every available space.
questions.correctAnswer: It usually keeps its own shape and volume.
questions.reviewNote: A solid keeps shape and volume.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a liquid?
choices: It keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container.
It keeps one shape no matter where it is placed.
It has no volume because it can be poured.
questions.correctAnswer: It keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container.
questions.reviewNote: A liquid flows and takes the container's shape.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a gas?
choices: It spreads out to fill the space available.
It always stays at the bottom of a container.
It keeps the same shape as a cube.
questions.correctAnswer: It spreads out to fill the space available.

questions.prompt: In a simple model, particles in a solid are usually...
choices: close together and mostly vibrating in place
far apart and moving freely through a room
spaced like a liquid but with no volume
questions.correctAnswer: close together and mostly vibrating in place

questions.prompt: Why can liquid water take the shape of a glass?
choices: Its particles can move past one another.
Its particles stop being matter inside glass.
Its particles become a gas when poured.
questions.correctAnswer: Its particles can move past one another.
questions.reviewNote: Liquid particles can slide past one another.

questions.prompt: Which particle description best fits a gas?
choices: Particles are far apart and move freely.
Particles are packed in a fixed pattern.
Particles have no motion at all.
questions.correctAnswer: Particles are far apart and move freely.

questions.prompt: Air is matter even though it is not easy to see.
choices: True
False
questions.reviewNote: Air has mass and takes up space.

questions.prompt: Shape and volume can help identify a state of matter.
choices: True
False
questions.reviewNote: Shape and volume are useful clues.

lessons.title: Changes of State
lessons.learningGoal: Students will explain melting, freezing, evaporation, and condensation as changes of state caused by heating or cooling.
successCriteria: I can name common changes of state.
I can connect heating and cooling to changes of state.
I can explain that a change of state does not usually make a new substance.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise identifying changes of state and explaining how heating or cooling affects matter.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that changes of state can change how matter behaves while the substance itself may stay the same.
lessons.christianFocus: Students study patterns in created matter with careful attention to cause and effect.
lessonContent: A change of state happens when matter changes between solid, liquid, and gas.
Melting changes a solid to a liquid.
Freezing changes a liquid to a solid.
Evaporation changes a liquid to a gas. Condensation changes a gas to a liquid.
Heating or cooling can change the state of matter, but the substance may still be the same material.

studentActivity.title: State Change Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise identifying changes of state and explaining the role of heating and cooling.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: matter can change state
steps.text: When matter changes between solid, liquid, and gas, it has changed state. The material may look different, but it may still be the same substance.

steps.title: Four Important Words
steps.prompt: Know the direction
steps.text: Melting changes solid to liquid. Freezing changes liquid to solid. Evaporation changes liquid to gas. Condensation changes gas to liquid.

steps.title: Melting
steps.prompt: An ice cube becomes liquid water on a warm counter. What change of state happened?
choices: melting
condensation
freezing
steps.feedback: Correct. Melting changes a solid to a liquid.
steps.hint: The ice started as a solid.

steps.title: Freezing
steps.prompt: Liquid water becomes ice in a freezer. What change of state happened?
choices: freezing
evaporation
melting
steps.feedback: Yes. Freezing changes a liquid to a solid.
steps.hint: The ending state is solid.

steps.title: Condensation
steps.prompt: Tiny water drops form on the outside of a cold glass. Which change is involved?
choices: condensation
melting
dissolving
steps.feedback: Correct. Water vapour in the air can cool and become liquid droplets.
steps.hint: Gas changing to liquid is the clue.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Evaporation changes a liquid into a gas.
choices: True
False
steps.feedback: Correct. Evaporation is liquid to gas.
steps.hint: Think of water slowly drying from a puddle.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised naming changes of state.

steps.title: Heating and Cooling
steps.prompt: Energy affects particle movement
steps.text: Heating usually makes particles move more, which can lead to melting or evaporation. Cooling usually makes particles move less, which can lead to freezing or condensation.

steps.title: Heating Example
steps.prompt: Which change usually happens when enough heat is added to ice?
choices: It melts into liquid water.
It freezes into harder ice.
It dissolves into air.
steps.feedback: Correct. Heating ice can cause melting.
steps.hint: Ice is solid water.

steps.title: Cooling Example
steps.prompt: Which change usually happens when water vapour cools on a cold surface?
choices: It condenses into liquid droplets.
It melts into a solid block.
It becomes salt.
steps.feedback: Yes. Cooling water vapour can cause condensation.
steps.hint: Gas to liquid is condensation.

steps.title: Same Substance
steps.prompt: Why is melting ice usually a physical change?
choices: The state changes, but the substance is still water.
The water changes into a new metal.
The water disappears from matter completely.
steps.correctAnswer: The state changes, but the substance is still water.
steps.feedback: Correct. Ice and liquid water are both water.
steps.hint: Ask whether a new substance formed.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Heating or cooling can change a material's state without making a new substance.
choices: True
False
steps.feedback: Correct. State changes usually keep the same substance.
steps.hint: Water is still water as ice, liquid water, or water vapour.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised explaining changes of state.

questions.prompt: What is melting?
choices: solid changing to liquid
liquid changing to solid
gas changing to liquid

questions.prompt: What is freezing?
choices: liquid changing to solid
solid changing to gas
gas changing to liquid

questions.prompt: A puddle slowly dries on a warm day. Which change is happening?
choices: evaporation
freezing
condensation
questions.reviewNote: Liquid water is becoming water vapour.

questions.prompt: Water drops form on a cold mirror after a warm shower. Which change is happening?
choices: condensation
melting
dissolving
questions.reviewNote: Water vapour cools and becomes liquid.

questions.prompt: What can enough heating do to a solid such as ice?
choices: cause it to melt
cause it to become a different element
cause it to stop taking up space

questions.prompt: What can enough cooling do to liquid water?
choices: cause it to freeze
cause it to become salt
cause it to lose all mass

questions.prompt: A change of state usually means a new substance has formed.
choices: True
False
questions.reviewNote: A state change often keeps the same substance.

questions.prompt: Water can exist as ice, liquid water, and water vapour.
choices: True
False
questions.reviewNote: Water can be solid, liquid, or gas.

lessons.title: Physical Changes
lessons.learningGoal: Students will identify physical changes and explain that physical changes do not make a new substance.
successCriteria: I can describe a physical change.
I can explain why some physical changes are easy to reverse and some are not.
I can compare physical changes with changes that may form new substances.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise identifying physical changes, including changes in size, shape, state, and mixtures.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that a physical change affects form or appearance without producing a new substance.
lessons.christianFocus: Students practise honest observation and careful reasoning when studying changes in the materials God made.
lessonContent: A physical change changes the form, size, shape, state, or arrangement of matter.
A physical change does not make a new substance.
Cutting, folding, crushing, melting, freezing, and many kinds of mixing are physical changes.
Some physical changes are easy to reverse, but a change can be physical even if it is not easy to reverse.
The key question is whether a new substance formed.

studentActivity.title: Physical Change Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise deciding whether a change is physical and explaining your evidence.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: form can change
steps.text: A physical change changes how matter looks or behaves, but it does not make a new substance. The material is still the same kind of matter.

steps.title: Not Always Easy to Reverse
steps.prompt: Reversibility is not the only clue
steps.text: Melting ice is easy to reverse by freezing. Cutting paper is harder to reverse, but it is still a physical change because the paper did not become a new substance.

steps.title: Cut Paper
steps.prompt: Why is cutting paper usually a physical change?
choices: The size and shape change, but the paper remains paper.
The paper becomes a new chemical substance.
The paper stops being matter because it is smaller.
steps.correctAnswer: The size and shape change, but the paper remains paper.
steps.feedback: Correct. The paper's form changed, not its substance.
steps.hint: Ask whether a new substance formed.

steps.title: Melting Chocolate
steps.prompt: Chocolate melts in a warm room. Which explanation is best?
choices: Its state changes, but it is still chocolate.
It changes into a gas because it is warm.
It becomes a new metal because heat was added.
steps.correctAnswer: Its state changes, but it is still chocolate.
steps.feedback: Yes. Melting is a physical change.
steps.hint: Melting changes state.

steps.title: Mixture
steps.prompt: Sand and water are stirred together. Why is this usually a physical change?
choices: The materials are mixed but no new substance is made.
The sand becomes part of the water molecules.
The water changes into a solid rock.
steps.correctAnswer: The materials are mixed but no new substance is made.
steps.feedback: Correct. Mixing can be a physical change.
steps.hint: The sand and water are still sand and water.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A physical change must always be easy to undo.
choices: True
False
steps.feedback: Correct. Some physical changes are not easy to reverse.
steps.hint: Cutting paper is not easy to undo, but it is physical.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised spotting physical changes.

steps.title: Use the New Substance Question
steps.prompt: Evidence matters
steps.text: When deciding whether a change is physical, ask: Did the material only change form, size, shape, state, or arrangement? Or did it make a new substance?

steps.title: Dissolving Sugar
steps.prompt: Sugar dissolves in water. Which explanation is most accurate?
choices: The sugar spreads evenly in the water, but the sugar has not simply vanished.
The sugar stops being matter as soon as it cannot be seen.
The water changes the sugar into sand.
steps.correctAnswer: The sugar spreads evenly in the water, but the sugar has not simply vanished.
steps.feedback: Correct. Dissolving is often a physical change.
steps.hint: Not seeing something does not mean it is gone.

steps.title: Physical or Chemical
steps.prompt: Which change is most clearly physical?
choices: crushing a piece of chalk into powder
rust forming on an iron nail
wood burning in a fire
steps.correctAnswer: crushing a piece of chalk into powder
steps.feedback: Yes. The chalk changes size and shape but remains chalk.
steps.hint: Look for a change in form without a new substance.

steps.title: Best Evidence
steps.prompt: A student says a change is physical. Which evidence best supports that claim?
choices: The material changed shape but kept the same substance.
The material looked different and was surprising.
The material was hard to put back exactly as it was.
steps.correctAnswer: The material changed shape but kept the same substance.
steps.feedback: Correct. Same substance is the important evidence.
steps.hint: A change can look different without making a new substance.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: If matter changes from solid to liquid, it has always formed a new substance.
choices: True
False
steps.feedback: Correct. Melting usually keeps the same substance.
steps.hint: Think about ice and liquid water.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised explaining physical changes.

questions.prompt: What happens during a physical change?
choices: Matter changes form or appearance without making a new substance.
Matter must become a completely different substance.
Matter loses all properties and cannot be described.
questions.correctAnswer: Matter changes form or appearance without making a new substance.
questions.reviewNote: Physical changes do not make new substances.

questions.prompt: Why is cutting cardboard usually a physical change?
choices: The shape changes, but the cardboard remains cardboard.
The cardboard becomes a new gas.
The cardboard stops having mass.
questions.correctAnswer: The shape changes, but the cardboard remains cardboard.

questions.prompt: Which change is physical?
choices: ice melting into liquid water
iron rusting after being left outside
paper burning into ash and smoke

questions.prompt: Sugar dissolves in water. Which idea is most accurate?
choices: The sugar particles are spread through the water.
The sugar has stopped existing because it cannot be seen.
The water has turned the sugar into glass.
questions.correctAnswer: The sugar particles are spread through the water.

questions.prompt: Which statement about physical changes is correct?
choices: Some are easy to reverse, and some are not.
All physical changes are impossible to reverse.
Every physical change forms a new substance.
questions.correctAnswer: Some are easy to reverse, and some are not.
questions.reviewNote: Reversibility is helpful but not the only clue.

questions.prompt: Which question is most useful when identifying a physical change?
choices: Did a new substance form?
Did the material look less useful?
Did the material become harder to describe?
questions.reviewNote: New substance formation is the key question.

questions.prompt: Crushing a cracker into crumbs is usually a physical change.
choices: True
False
questions.reviewNote: The size and shape change, but the substance remains cracker.

questions.prompt: A change must be easy to undo in order to be physical.
choices: True
False
questions.reviewNote: Some physical changes are difficult to reverse.

lessons.title: Chemical Changes
lessons.learningGoal: Students will identify evidence that a chemical change may have formed a new substance.
successCriteria: I can explain what a chemical change is.
I can identify signs that a new substance may have formed.
I can remember that one sign alone may not prove a chemical change.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise recognizing chemical changes and using evidence carefully.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that a chemical change forms one or more new substances and that signs of chemical change should be interpreted carefully.
lessons.christianFocus: Students should use careful evidence and safe habits when studying chemical changes in God's created world.
lessonContent: A chemical change happens when one or more new substances form.
Possible signs include gas bubbles, a colour change, heat or light being produced, a new odour, or a new solid forming.
A sign is a clue, not always proof by itself. For example, boiling water has bubbles but is still a physical change.
Rusting, burning, baking, and some reactions between substances are examples of chemical changes.
Chemical investigations should be done only with teacher-approved materials and safety instructions.

studentActivity.title: Chemical Change Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise using evidence to decide whether a chemical change may have happened.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: look for new substances
steps.text: A chemical change forms one or more new substances. The new substance may have different properties from the starting materials.

steps.title: Signs Are Clues
steps.prompt: Do not jump too quickly
steps.text: Gas bubbles, colour change, heat, light, new odour, or a new solid can be signs of chemical change. But one sign alone may not prove it, because some physical changes can look similar.

steps.title: Rusting
steps.prompt: An iron nail is left damp and reddish-brown rust forms. What kind of change is this?
choices: chemical change
change of state
simple dissolving
steps.feedback: Correct. Rust is a new substance.
steps.hint: Ask whether a new substance formed.

steps.title: Baking
steps.prompt: Dough is baked and becomes bread with new smell, texture, and colour. Which explanation is best?
choices: Chemical changes helped form new substances in the bread.
The dough only changed container shape.
The dough simply froze and melted at the same time.
steps.correctAnswer: Chemical changes helped form new substances in the bread.
steps.feedback: Yes. Baking involves chemical changes.
steps.hint: Think about new properties after heating.

steps.title: Gas Clue
steps.prompt: Two safe classroom liquids are mixed by the teacher and bubbles form. What is the careful conclusion?
choices: Gas bubbles may be evidence of a chemical change, but the whole situation should be checked.
Bubbles always prove the substance is boiling.
Bubbles mean the mixture is no longer matter.
steps.correctAnswer: Gas bubbles may be evidence of a chemical change, but the whole situation should be checked.
steps.feedback: Correct. Bubbles can be a clue, but evidence should be checked carefully.
steps.hint: A clue is helpful, but not always proof alone.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A chemical change forms one or more new substances.
choices: True
False
steps.feedback: Correct. New substance formation is the key idea.
steps.hint: Chemical changes change substance identity.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised spotting chemical change clues.

steps.title: Compare With Physical Changes
steps.prompt: Some clues need checking
steps.text: Boiling water makes bubbles, but it is still water changing from liquid to gas. A chemical change needs evidence that a new substance formed.

steps.title: Bubbles in Boiling
steps.prompt: Water boils in a kettle and bubbles rise. Why is this not enough to prove a chemical change?
choices: The bubbles are water vapour forming during a change of state.
Boiling removes all matter from the kettle.
Bubbles only happen when rust forms.
steps.correctAnswer: The bubbles are water vapour forming during a change of state.
steps.feedback: Correct. Boiling is a physical change of state.
steps.hint: The substance is still water.

steps.title: Best Evidence
steps.prompt: Which observation gives the strongest evidence that a new substance may have formed?
choices: A new solid appears after two clear liquids are mixed.
A block is cut into two smaller pieces.
Water is poured into a taller container.
steps.correctAnswer: A new solid appears after two clear liquids are mixed.
steps.feedback: Yes. A new solid can be evidence of a chemical change.
steps.hint: The new solid is called a precipitate.

steps.title: Safety
steps.prompt: What should students do before mixing materials in a science investigation?
choices: follow teacher-approved instructions and safety rules
taste a tiny amount to identify it
mix larger amounts to make the result clearer
steps.correctAnswer: follow teacher-approved instructions and safety rules
steps.feedback: Correct. Chemical investigations require careful safety.
steps.hint: Unknown materials should never be tasted.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A colour change can be a clue for a chemical change, but it should be considered with other evidence.
choices: True
False
steps.feedback: Correct. A colour change is a clue, not always proof by itself.
steps.hint: Careful scientists use several pieces of evidence.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised using chemical change evidence carefully.

questions.prompt: What happens during a chemical change?
choices: One or more new substances form.
Only the shape changes while the substance stays the same.
Matter stops having mass and volume.
questions.correctAnswer: One or more new substances form.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a chemical change?
choices: rust forming on iron
ice melting in a cup
paper being folded in half

questions.prompt: Which can be a sign of chemical change?
choices: a new gas, new solid, colour change, heat, light, or odour
only a change in container shape
only a material being moved to a new table
questions.correctAnswer: a new gas, new solid, colour change, heat, light, or odour
questions.reviewNote: These can be clues that a new substance formed.

questions.prompt: Why do bubbles not always prove a chemical change?
choices: Boiling water also makes bubbles during a physical change.
Bubbles can only happen in solids.
Bubbles mean the matter has no particles.
questions.correctAnswer: Boiling water also makes bubbles during a physical change.
questions.reviewNote: Bubbles are clues that need context.

questions.prompt: Why can baking dough involve chemical changes?
choices: New substances with different properties can form.
The dough only changes its container.
The dough simply becomes colder.
questions.correctAnswer: New substances with different properties can form.

questions.prompt: Which safety rule is best for chemical investigations?
choices: Use only teacher-approved materials and instructions.
Taste unknown materials if they look safe.
Mix extra amounts to make a larger reaction.
questions.correctAnswer: Use only teacher-approved materials and instructions.

questions.prompt: A new substance forming is the key idea in a chemical change.
choices: True
False
questions.reviewNote: That is the main difference from a physical change.

questions.prompt: Every colour change automatically proves a chemical change.
choices: True
False
questions.reviewNote: A colour change is a clue, but evidence should be checked.

lessons.title: Mixtures and Solutions
lessons.learningGoal: Students will compare mixtures and solutions and explain what happens when a substance dissolves.
successCriteria: I can describe a mixture.
I can describe a solution as a special kind of mixture.
I can explain that a dissolved substance is still present.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise distinguishing mixtures from solutions and explaining dissolving.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that mixtures contain substances together and that solutions are mixtures with a substance dissolved evenly.
lessons.christianFocus: Students practise careful stewardship by using materials thoughtfully and avoiding waste during investigations.
lessonContent: A mixture contains two or more substances together.
A solution is a special kind of mixture where one substance dissolves evenly in another.
The solute is the substance that dissolves. The solvent is the substance that does the dissolving.
Salt water and sugar water are common examples of solutions.
When a substance dissolves, it may become hard to see, but it has not simply disappeared.
practiceIdeas: Share the student mission for practice stars.
Use the lesson quiz as the scored check.
Review missed ideas before assigning the next Properties and Changes of Matter lesson.

studentActivityPlan.description: Practise comparing mixtures, solutions, solutes, and solvents.
studentActivityPlan.reward: 10 practice stars after each completed level

quizPlan.title: Mixtures and Solutions Quiz
quizPlan.format: Multiple choice and true/false questions with one score at the end.
quizPlan.focus: Mixtures, solutions, dissolving, solute, solvent, and separation ideas

lessons.assessmentPlan: Use the activity to build confidence and the quiz to check independent understanding.

studentActivity.title: Mixtures and Solutions Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise comparing mixtures, solutions, solutes, and solvents.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: substances can be combined
steps.text: A mixture contains two or more substances together. Some mixtures are easy to see, like trail mix. Other mixtures may look the same throughout.

steps.title: Solutions Are Special Mixtures
steps.prompt: Dissolved evenly
steps.text: A solution forms when one substance dissolves evenly in another. In salt water, salt is the solute and water is the solvent.

steps.title: Mixture
steps.prompt: Which is the best example of a mixture?
choices: sand and small pebbles together
a single ice cube made of water
one clean copper wire
steps.feedback: Correct. Sand and pebbles are substances together.
steps.hint: Look for two or more substances combined.

steps.title: Solution
steps.prompt: Which is the best example of a solution?
choices: sugar dissolved evenly in water
dry rice mixed with dry beans
marbles sorted by colour
steps.feedback: Yes. Sugar water is a solution.
steps.hint: A solution is mixed evenly after dissolving.

steps.title: Not a Solution
steps.prompt: Why is sand mixed with water usually not a solution?
choices: The sand does not dissolve evenly in the water.
The water stops being matter when sand is added.
The sand becomes invisible after one stir.
steps.correctAnswer: The sand does not dissolve evenly in the water.
steps.feedback: Correct. Sand usually settles instead of dissolving.
steps.hint: Solutions involve dissolving.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A solution is a kind of mixture.
choices: True
False
steps.feedback: Correct. A solution is a special mixture.
steps.hint: Solutions contain substances together.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised comparing mixtures and solutions.

steps.title: Solute and Solvent
steps.prompt: Name the parts
steps.text: The solute is the substance that dissolves. The solvent is the substance that does the dissolving. In most classroom examples, water is the solvent.

steps.title: Solute
steps.prompt: In salt water, what is the solute?
choices: salt
water
the glass
steps.feedback: Correct. Salt is the substance being dissolved.
steps.hint: The solute dissolves.

steps.title: Solvent
steps.prompt: In sugar water, what is the solvent?
choices: water
sugar
the spoon
steps.feedback: Yes. Water does the dissolving.
steps.hint: The solvent is the substance that dissolves another substance.

steps.title: Still Present
steps.prompt: A student says, 'The salt disappeared when it dissolved.' Which response is most accurate?
choices: The salt is still present but spread through the water.
The salt stopped being matter because it cannot be seen.
The salt turned into empty space between water particles.
steps.correctAnswer: The salt is still present but spread through the water.
steps.feedback: Correct. Dissolved substances are still present.
steps.hint: Dissolved does not mean gone.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: If a substance dissolves, it may be hard to see but it is still part of the solution.
choices: True
False
steps.feedback: Correct. Dissolved substances are still there.
steps.hint: Think about tasting salt in salt water, though students should not taste unknown mixtures.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised explaining dissolving.

questions.prompt: What is a mixture?
choices: two or more substances together
only one substance with no other material
a material that has no properties

questions.prompt: What is a solution?
choices: a mixture where one substance dissolves evenly in another
a mixture where all parts must be large enough to pick up
a solid that changes shape but not volume
questions.correctAnswer: a mixture where one substance dissolves evenly in another
questions.reviewNote: A solution is an evenly mixed dissolved mixture.

questions.prompt: Which is most likely a solution?
choices: salt dissolved in water
sand settled at the bottom of water
buttons sorted into a jar

questions.prompt: Why is gravel in water not usually a solution?
choices: The gravel does not dissolve evenly.
The water has no volume after gravel is added.
The gravel becomes a gas immediately.
questions.correctAnswer: The gravel does not dissolve evenly.

questions.prompt: What is the solute in sugar water?
choices: sugar
water
cup

questions.prompt: What is the solvent in salt water?
choices: water
salt
spoon

questions.prompt: A dissolved substance has simply stopped existing.
choices: True
False
questions.reviewNote: A dissolved substance is still present.

questions.prompt: Solutions are mixtures, but not all mixtures are solutions.
choices: True
False
questions.reviewNote: A solution is a special kind of mixture.

lessons.title: Separating Mixtures Responsibly
lessons.learningGoal: Students will choose suitable methods for separating mixtures based on material properties.
successCriteria: I can match separation methods to material properties.
I can explain why filtering, sieving, magnetism, settling, or evaporation may work.
I can choose safe and responsible habits when using materials.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise choosing separation methods and using materials responsibly.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that mixtures can often be separated by using differences in properties.
lessons.christianFocus: Students connect science choices with stewardship by using materials carefully, avoiding waste, and following safe disposal instructions.
lessonContent: Many mixtures can be separated by using differences in properties.
A magnet can separate magnetic materials from non-magnetic materials.
A sieve or filter can separate materials by particle size or by whether a solid stays behind.
Settling and careful pouring can help separate some mixtures.
Evaporation can help recover a dissolved solid from a solution, but it should be done only with teacher-approved materials.
Responsible science uses small amounts, avoids waste, and follows safety and disposal instructions.
practiceIdeas: Share the student mission for practice stars.
Use the lesson quiz as the scored check.
Review missed ideas before assigning the next Properties and Changes of Matter lesson.

studentActivityPlan.title: Separate It Safely Mission
studentActivityPlan.description: Practise choosing safe methods to separate mixtures.
studentActivityPlan.reward: 10 practice stars after each completed level

quizPlan.title: Separating Mixtures Responsibly Quiz
quizPlan.format: Multiple choice and true/false questions with one score at the end.
quizPlan.focus: Separation methods, material properties, safety, stewardship, and responsible disposal

lessons.assessmentPlan: Use the activity to build confidence and the quiz to check independent understanding.

studentActivity.title: Separate It Safely Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise choosing safe methods to separate mixtures.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: properties guide the method
steps.text: To separate a mixture, look for a property difference. One part might be magnetic, larger, smaller, insoluble, floating, settled, or dissolved.

steps.title: Common Methods
steps.prompt: Match method to evidence
steps.text: Magnets separate magnetic materials. Sieves separate by size. Filters can catch some solids. Evaporation can leave dissolved solids behind after water changes to vapour.

steps.title: Magnetism
steps.prompt: A mixture contains sand and iron filings. Which method is most useful?
choices: using a magnet
waiting for evaporation
measuring the temperature
steps.feedback: Correct. Iron filings are magnetic.
steps.hint: Use the property that is different.

steps.title: Particle Size
steps.prompt: A mixture contains gravel and fine sand. Which method would likely work best?
choices: using a sieve
using a thermometer
adding more water until both dissolve
steps.feedback: Yes. A sieve can separate by particle size.
steps.hint: Gravel and fine sand have different sizes.

steps.title: Filtering
steps.prompt: Muddy water contains solid soil particles. Which method may help remove many solids?
choices: filtering
checking magnetism only
freezing the cup without looking
steps.feedback: Correct. A filter can trap some solid particles.
steps.hint: Think about solid particles being caught.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: The best separation method depends on the properties of the materials in the mixture.
choices: True
False
steps.feedback: Correct. Properties guide the method.
steps.hint: Different mixtures need different methods.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised choosing separation methods.

steps.title: Responsible Science
steps.prompt: Use materials wisely
steps.text: Good science includes stewardship. Use only the amount needed, keep unknown materials away from mouths and eyes, and follow instructions for cleanup and disposal.

steps.title: Evaporation
steps.prompt: A teacher wants students to recover salt from salt water. Which method fits the property difference?
choices: evaporating the water with approved equipment
using a magnet on the salt water
sieving the liquid through a large mesh
steps.correctAnswer: evaporating the water with approved equipment
steps.feedback: Correct. Evaporation can leave dissolved salt behind.
steps.hint: The salt is dissolved, so size sorting will not work well.

steps.title: Settling
steps.prompt: A jar has water and a heavy insoluble solid. After time, the solid sinks. What helped separate it?
choices: settling because of differences in how the materials behave in water
condensation because gas became liquid
magnetism because all solids are magnetic
steps.correctAnswer: settling because of differences in how the materials behave in water
steps.feedback: Yes. Settling can separate some insoluble solids.
steps.hint: The solid sinks instead of dissolving.

steps.title: Stewardship
steps.prompt: Which choice shows responsible material use?
choices: use small amounts and follow cleanup instructions
pour unknown mixtures down the sink without asking
mix extra materials to make the investigation look bigger
steps.correctAnswer: use small amounts and follow cleanup instructions
steps.feedback: Correct. Responsible science avoids waste and follows safety directions.
steps.hint: Think about safety and stewardship.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Students should never taste unknown materials during a separation investigation.
choices: True
False
steps.feedback: Correct. Unknown materials should not be tasted.
steps.hint: Safety comes first.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised separating mixtures responsibly.

questions.prompt: Which method is best for separating iron filings from sand?
choices: using a magnet
evaporating the sand
measuring the colour of both materials

questions.prompt: Which method is best for separating gravel from fine sand?
choices: using a sieve
using a magnet only
condensing water vapour
questions.reviewNote: A sieve separates by particle size.

questions.prompt: Which method may help remove solid particles from muddy water?
choices: filtering
folding
melting
questions.reviewNote: A filter can catch some solids.

questions.prompt: How could salt be recovered from salt water with teacher-approved equipment?
choices: evaporate the water and leave salt behind
use a magnet to pull out dissolved salt
sieve the solution through a large mesh
questions.correctAnswer: evaporate the water and leave salt behind
questions.reviewNote: Evaporation can leave dissolved solids behind.

questions.prompt: Why might settling help separate a mixture?
choices: One solid may sink instead of dissolving.
Every solution forms a new gas.
All liquids become magnetic over time.
questions.correctAnswer: One solid may sink instead of dissolving.
questions.reviewNote: Settling works when materials behave differently in water.

questions.prompt: Which habit shows responsible science?
choices: use small amounts and follow disposal instructions
throw mixed materials anywhere after testing
taste materials to find out what they are
questions.correctAnswer: use small amounts and follow disposal instructions

questions.prompt: A separation method should be chosen based on material properties.
choices: True
False

questions.prompt: Unknown materials should not be tasted during investigations.
choices: True
False

lessons.title: Unit 3 Final Quiz
lessons.teacherSummary: The Unit 3 final quiz checks properties of matter, states of matter, changes of state, physical changes, chemical changes, mixtures, solutions, separation methods, and responsible material use.
lessons.teacherOverview: Use this quiz after students complete the Properties and Changes of Matter lessons.

quiz.title: Properties and Changes of Matter Unit Quiz

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes matter?
choices: Anything that has mass and takes up space.
Only things that are solid and can be held.
Only objects that are made by people.
questions.correctAnswer: Anything that has mass and takes up space.

questions.prompt: Which description uses properties well?
choices: The material is rough, flexible, and dark green.
The material is the best choice because I like it.
The material probably came from a store.
questions.correctAnswer: The material is rough, flexible, and dark green.

questions.prompt: Which property describes whether a substance dissolves?
choices: solubility
magnetism
transparency

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a solid?
choices: It usually keeps its own shape and volume.
It takes the shape of its container and spreads everywhere.
It has no particles if it cannot be poured.
questions.correctAnswer: It usually keeps its own shape and volume.
questions.reviewNote: Solids usually keep shape and volume.

questions.prompt: Water is poured from a bottle into a bowl. What usually changes?
choices: its shape
the fact that it has volume
the substance it is made of
questions.reviewNote: A liquid takes the shape of its container.

questions.prompt: Which particle model best fits a gas?
choices: particles far apart and moving freely
particles packed closely in a fixed pattern
particles close together but sliding slowly
questions.correctAnswer: particles far apart and moving freely
questions.reviewNote: Gas particles are farther apart and move freely.

questions.prompt: Ice becoming liquid water is called...
choices: melting
freezing
condensation

questions.prompt: Water drops forming from cooled water vapour is called...
choices: condensation
dissolving
sieving

questions.prompt: Why is freezing water usually a physical change?
choices: The state changes, but the substance is still water.
Water changes into a new metal.
Water stops being matter when it freezes.
questions.correctAnswer: The state changes, but the substance is still water.

questions.prompt: Why is cutting paper usually a physical change?
choices: The size and shape change, but the paper remains paper.
A new substance forms every time paper is cut.
The paper becomes a gas because it has more edges.
questions.correctAnswer: The size and shape change, but the paper remains paper.

questions.prompt: What happens when sugar dissolves in water?
choices: The sugar is spread through the water but is still present.
The sugar stops existing because it cannot be seen.
The water changes the sugar into air.
questions.correctAnswer: The sugar is spread through the water but is still present.

questions.prompt: Which statement about physical changes is correct?
choices: A physical change can be hard to reverse and still be physical.
A physical change always creates a new substance.
A physical change means matter loses its volume.
questions.correctAnswer: A physical change can be hard to reverse and still be physical.
questions.reviewNote: Reversibility is not the only clue.

questions.prompt: What is the key idea in a chemical change?
choices: One or more new substances form.
Matter only moves to a new container.
The material must become easier to see.
questions.correctAnswer: One or more new substances form.

questions.prompt: Which change is chemical?
choices: rust forming on iron
ice melting on a plate
sand being mixed with pebbles

questions.prompt: Why do bubbles not always prove a chemical change?
choices: Boiling also makes bubbles during a physical state change.
Bubbles only happen when matter disappears.
Bubbles are never useful evidence in science.
questions.correctAnswer: Boiling also makes bubbles during a physical state change.
questions.reviewNote: Bubbles are clues that need context.

questions.prompt: What is a mixture?
choices: two or more substances together
one substance with no other material
matter with no measurable properties

questions.prompt: Which example is a solution?
choices: salt dissolved evenly in water
gravel settled in a jar of water
pencils sorted by length

questions.prompt: In sugar water, what is the solute?
choices: sugar
water
cup

questions.prompt: Which method best separates gravel from fine sand?
choices: sieving
condensation
measuring temperature
questions.reviewNote: A sieve separates by particle size.

questions.prompt: Which choice shows responsible science?
choices: use small amounts and follow cleanup instructions
taste a mixture if it looks familiar
pour unknown materials away without asking
questions.correctAnswer: use small amounts and follow cleanup instructions
questions.reviewNote: Responsible science includes safety and stewardship.
